node.label: Carolyn Merchant
node.date_label: The Death of Nature 1980 · Ecological Revolutions 1989 · Radical Ecology 1992 · coverage through 2000
node.description: A historian of science and environmental historian who argued in The Death of Nature (1980) that a science 'reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women'. In Ecological Revolutions (1989), a study of New England from 1600 to 1860, she treated major changes in human relations with nature as arising from tensions 'between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction', which in turn reshape consciousness. Answering Worster's three levels of ecology, production and cognition in 1990, she wrote that environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' and a gender analysis of each level. Her reading of Bacon's metaphors was disputed in the 1990s (Soble 1995; Pesic 1999, whom she answered in 2006), and a 1991 reviewer, praising her integration of gender, found 'painfully few people making history' in the New England book.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Carolyn Merchant (b. 1936); The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980); “The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions” (1987); Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (1989); “Gender and Environmental History” (JAH round table, 1990); Radical Ecology: The Search for a Livable World (1992). Readings: Cronon (1993); Steinberg's review (1991); Soble (1995); Leach and Green (1997); Pesic (1999); Merchant's own retrospectives (1998, 2006).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Merchant's framework as her own in-period texts state it: the 1987 Environmental Review article and the 1990 JAH response (both read in full, original pagination); The Death of Nature (1980) and Ecological Revolutions (1989) through author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'); and the 1992 conclusion to Radical Ecology (facsimile, original pages). She is not presented as the founder of environmental history or of ecofeminism. She builds on Kuhn and on Marx and Engels, on Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal for reproduction, and on Worster's levels; in 1998 she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin ('It was Kubrin’s idea that the key concept of early modern science was that matter was dead'). She separates her socialist ecofeminism from a radical feminism that 'runs the risk of perpetuating the very value hierarchies it seeks to overthrow' (1989). The Bacon reading is contested (Soble 1995 and Pesic 1999, abstracts only), Leach and Green (1997) place The Death of Nature among the ecofeminist histories they criticise, and Steinberg (1991) faults the New England book's narrative. McNeill (2003) and Merchant's 2006 Isis response are later readings, not evidence for the 1980–1992 framework.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ecological revolutions: tensions between ecology, production and reproduction reshape consciousness of nature, with gender analysed at every level (1987–1990)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Merchant's own statement of the framework, 'The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions', Environmental Review 11:4 (1987), read in full: 'My thesis is that ecological revolutions are major transformations in human relations with non-human nature. They arise from changes, tensions, and contradictions that develop between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction. Those dynamics in turn support the acceptance of new forms of consciousness, ideas, images, and world views' (pp. 265–266). 'The concepts most useful for this approach to environmental history are ecology, production, reproduction, and consciousness' (p. 267); 'An ecological approach to history asserts the idea of nature as a historical actor' (p. 267); production is twofold, 'reproduction is fourfold, having both biological and social articulations' (p. 270); 'Under capitalist patriarchy, reproduction is subordinate to production' (p. 271). Ecological Revolutions (1989), chapter 1 (reprint, Dolbeare 1996, p. 578): in each revolution 'The relations between men and women through which daily life was maintained and reproduced were radically changed.' In the 1990 JAH round table she writes that Worster's essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and that 'environmental history needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction, which interacts with the other three levels' (p. 1117); shifts of power are 'not only those between indigenous and invading cultures but also those between men and women' (p. 1121). In-period readings: Steinberg (Technology and Culture, 1991, read in full) calls her theorizing, 'especially its integration of gender into the analysis', 'a signal contribution', but adds 'There are painfully few people making history in this book' (p. 399); Cronon (1993) footnotes to Death of Nature and Ecological Revolutions the lesson that one cannot understand how a culture relates to an environment 'without examining the ways it engenders the natural world' (p. 9, n. 18). A contribution, not a founding: she takes Kuhn's and Marx's theories of revolution as 'starting points' and rejects 'the determinism Marx assigns to the economic base' (1987, p. 266), draws reproduction from Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal (pp. 270–271), and adds to Worster's levels rather than replacing them (1990, p. 1117). McNeill (2003, pp. 38–39) is a later reading: the scheme 'has not attracted wide imitation within environmental history'.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: merchant_material_ideas ('Material change, ideas and gendered nature'; 'Her socialist ecofeminism addresses production and reproduction') holds her alone and names exactly the production–reproduction–consciousness scheme checked here. gender_nature ('Gender, science and the control of nature') rests on The Death of Nature and fits the science edge better. The strand's works line names Death of Nature and Radical Ecology; a reviewer may add Ecological Revolutions (1989) and the 1987 and 1990 articles.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Death of Nature: the mechanical philosophy's dead, inert nature legitimated manipulation and the domination of nature and women (1980)
proposed_edges.map_label: Mechanism and the death of nature, 1980
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Merchant's own argument, The Death of Nature (1980), read in two author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'). Introduction (Zimmerman, ed., Environmental Philosophy, 1993): 'The ancient identity of nature as a nurturing mother links women’s history with the history of the environment and ecological change'; we must reexamine 'a world view and a science that, by reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women' (p. 269); 'Two new ideas, those of mechanism and of the domination and mastery of nature, became core concepts of the modern world' (p. 270). On Bacon: he 'fashioned a new ethic sanctioning the exploitation of nature', though 'Bacon, of course, was not responsible for subsequent uses of his philosophy'; his courtroom imagery 'treats nature as a female to be tortured through mechanical inventions' (p. 272). Chapter excerpt (Zerzan and Carnes, eds., 1991, from 1980 pp. 192–193, 290–292, 294–295): 'Order and power together constituted control' (p. 36); 'The removal of animistic, organic assumptions about the cosmos constituted the death of nature—the most far-reaching effect of the Scientific Revolution', the mechanical order carrying 'a framework of values based on power, fully compatible with the directions taken by commercial capitalism' (p. 37). In-period reading: Cronon (1993, p. 3): 'Carolyn Merchant joined Worster in bringing an environmentalist perspective to the history of science, but combined it with a more feminist approach to argue in The Death of Nature that western science has harmed nature and women in parallel ways'. Contested: Merchant's 1998 retrospective reports early objections over 'how historical events were related to each other and especially to ideas' and 'the precise relationship between female metaphors that described nature and the social subjection of women' (p. 201). Soble (1995, abstract read) names Merchant among critics who claim 'misogynous sexual metaphors played an important role in the rise of modern science' and 'offers a defense of Bacon'; Pesic (1999, abstract read) holds that 'a close study of his works contradicts' the claim that Bacon advocated torturing nature. Leach and Green (1997, pp. 346, 348) place the book among ecofeminist histories in which 'femininity is linked a priori both “with nature” and “with the past”'; their main target is Shiva. A contribution, not a founding: she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin (1998, pp. 199–200). Merchant's 2006 Isis response is a later reading.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: women_environment ('Women, scientific careers, and environments') pairs Merchant's interpretation of nature with Rossiter's career history, and its focus already distinguishes the two questions; Merchant's part is the argument checked here. bacon_metaphor_dispute pairs her with Pesic and is about the disagreement, which this edge records in its evidence rather than as its claim; it also leans on the 2006 response, a later reading. Choose bacon_metaphor_dispute instead if reviewers want the arrow to land on the contested reading.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Considered on her own words: the Death of Nature introduction says nature as nurturing mother 'links women’s history with the history of the environment' (1993 reprint, p. 269), and the 1990 JAH piece recovers women conservationists ('the efforts of thousands of women were directly responsible for many of the country’s most significant conservation achievements', p. 1119) and women's changing roles in production. But the checked texts bring women and gender into environmental history and the history of science; no in-period women's-history text was read that takes her framework up, she has no women roster row, and no women strand fits (socialist_feminism holds British labour historians). edge_113 (environment → women) already carries the link with her name. Not proposed. If the editor wants it, the 1984 Environmental Review article 'Women of the Progressive Conservation Movement' (author-hosted, articles/17.pdf, unread) is the text to check, and edge_113 should then be relabelled as edge_336 is below.

The 1990 JAH response is titled 'Gender and Environmental History' and traces 'changes in forms of patriarchy' (p. 1120), and Steinberg (1991) praises her 'integration of gender into the analysis'. Both describe a contribution to environmental history. No checked text places her in gender history as a field (the gender node's strands are Scott, Davidoff and Hall, Stoler and others), and she has no gender roster row. Not proposed.

Radical Ecology (1992) is environmental philosophy and movement analysis; Cronon calls it 'less historical' (1993, p. 3). Its conclusion is cited only to show the framework extended (p. 239). No atlas field for environmental ethics was checked. Not proposed.

proposed.relationship: Histories of the Scientific Revolution and of ideas of nature taken into environmental history
proposed.map_label: Scientific Revolution and ideas of nature
proposed.evidence_note: History of science supplies environmental history with accounts of how ideas of nature were made and used, here the mechanical philosophy and the domination of nature. The Berkeley retrospective and the reprinted 1980 excerpt document the case mapped; Merchant's own contribution is the separate pair of edges from her person entry (revision 1.131). Pesic’s 1999 abstract supplies a competing reading of Bacon’s metaphor, and Merchant’s 2006 response is a later reading; they document disagreement and do not settle Bacon’s intentions.

new_sources.title: Carolyn Merchant, “The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions,” Environmental Review 11, no. 4 (Winter 1987): 265–274.
new_sources.citation: Carolyn Merchant, “The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions,” Environmental Review 11:4, special issue “Theories of Environmental History” (1987): 265–274. doi:10.2307/3984135.

verification.note: Read in full, pp. 265–274 with notes, from the author-hosted JSTOR scan (JSTOR stable 3984135; OpenAlex W2321626821). Thesis pp. 265–266; Kuhn and Marx as 'starting points' and Marx's 'determinism' rejected p. 266; ecology, production, reproduction and consciousness as the concepts of the approach, and 'nature as a historical actor', p. 267; Figure 1 (conceptual framework) p. 268; twofold production and fourfold reproduction pp. 270–271 (Meillassoux, Peterson, Bridenthal); 'Under capitalist patriarchy, reproduction is subordinate to production' p. 271; partible inheritance and landless sons pp. 271–272; consciousness, the 'primal gaze' and visual and analytic consciousness pp. 272–273; summary p. 273. Note 1 says the theory is drawn from her 'forthcoming book, Ecological Revolutions'. Her 1990 JAH note 2 cites this article as pp. 251–74; the article itself runs 265–274.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period statement of the ecological-revolutions framework in Merchant's own words.

new_sources.title: Carolyn Merchant, “Gender and Environmental History,” Journal of American History 76, no. 4 (March 1990): 1117–1121.
new_sources.citation: Carolyn Merchant, “Gender and Environmental History,” Journal of American History 76:4 (1990): 1117–1121, in the round table “Environmental History” responding to Donald Worster, “Transformations of the Earth.” doi:10.2307/2936589.

verification.note: Read in full, pp. 1117–1121 with notes, from the author-hosted JSTOR scan (JSTOR stable 2936589; OpenAlex W2326065961; OUP page gives pp. 1117–1121). Worster's essay 'lacks a gender analysis'; gender analysis of each of his three levels and 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117); women's and men's roles in production in subsistence, colonial and industrial economies (pp. 1117–1118); women conservationists, and 'the efforts of thousands of women were directly responsible for many of the country’s most significant conservation achievements' (p. 1119); cognition, nature as mother and the mechanistic framework (p. 1119); reproduction 'dialectically related to the other three' and its four aspects (p. 1120); forms of patriarchy and shifts of power 'between men and women'; 'both offers a more balanced and complete picture ... and advances its theoretical frameworks' (p. 1121). This is the round-table response the canon-evidence file could not access (item D); the other responses and Worster's reply remain unread.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period: Merchant's gender-and-reproduction addition to Worster's framework.

new_sources.title: Carolyn Merchant, Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1989).
new_sources.citation: Carolyn Merchant, Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1989), xv + 379 p.; excerpts from chapter 1 and the epilogue reprinted in Kenneth M. Dolbeare, ed., American Political Thought, 3rd ed. (Chatham, NJ: Chatham House, 1996), 577–590.

verification.note: Book itself unread (Internet Archive copies ecologicalrevolu00caro and ecologicalrevolu005 are lending-only; search-inside returned 403). Read instead: the author-hosted scan of the Dolbeare 1996 reprint, pp. 577–590, which reproduces parts of chapter 1 ('Ecology and History') and of the epilogue ('The Global Ecological Revolution'), credited 'Reprinted from ... Copyright © 1989 by the University of North Carolina Press'. Pages cited are the reprint's: two revolutions, and 'The relations between men and women through which daily life was maintained and reproduced were radically changed' (p. 578); the thesis, matching the 1987 article (p. 578); Kuhn and Marx (pp. 578–580); 'Nonhuman nature is an actor; human and nonhuman interactions constitute the drama' (pp. 584–585; page boundary uncertain in the two-page scan); a global ecological revolution would 'reconstruct gender relations between women and men and between humans and nature' (p. 589); radical feminism 'runs the risk of perpetuating the very value hierarchies it seeks to overthrow', socialist feminism views 'knowledge and reality as historically and socially constructed' (p. 590). Book pages 2–3, 143 and 187 are known only as quoted by Steinberg (1991). Edition: Steinberg's review gives UNC Press 1989, xv + 379 p.; Internet Archive metadata gives Chapel Hill, UNC Press, 1989; Open Library work OL2911252W.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period book, read through reprinted excerpts of the framework chapter and epilogue.

new_sources.title: Carolyn Merchant, The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980), introduction and chapter excerpts reprinted in Michael E. Zimmerman et al., eds., Environmental Philosophy: From Animal Rights to Radical Ecology (Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice Hall, 1993): 268–281.
new_sources.citation: Carolyn Merchant, “The Death of Nature,” excerpted from The Death of Nature (San Francisco: Harper & Row, 1980), in Zimmerman, Callicott, Sessions, Warren and Clark, eds., Environmental Philosophy (Prentice Hall, 1993), 268–281.

verification.note: Author-hosted scan (21 PDF pages) OCR'd and read: title, copyright and contents pages, and the excerpt pp. 268–281 with notes; the excerpt states it is 'Excerpted from The Death of Nature, originally published by Harper and Row (New York, 1980)'. It reproduces the introduction 'Women as Nature' (pp. 268–269), 'Nature as Female' (pp. 269–271) and 'Dominion over Nature: Francis Bacon’s Philosophy' (pp. 272–275), and further mechanism passages (pp. 276–280). Quoted: nature as nurturing mother 'links women’s history with the history of the environment'; a science that 'sanctioned the domination of both nature and women' (p. 269); mechanism and 'the domination and mastery of nature' as 'core concepts of the modern world' (p. 270); Bacon 'fashioned a new ethic sanctioning the exploitation of nature', 'was not responsible for subsequent uses of his philosophy', imagery that 'treats nature as a female to be tortured through mechanical inventions' (p. 272). Pages are the reprint's; 1980 pages are not assigned (Leach and Green 1997 cite the 'death of nature' sentence to p. xvii of the 1982 Wildwood House edition). The 1980 book itself is lending-only on the Internet Archive.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period book: its introduction and Bacon chapter in Merchant's words, via an authorised reprint.

new_sources.title: Carolyn Merchant, “Conclusion: The Radical Ecology Movement,” in Radical Ecology: The Search for a Livable World (New York: Routledge, 1992): 235–240.
new_sources.citation: Carolyn Merchant, Radical Ecology: The Search for a Livable World (New York and London: Routledge, 1992), conclusion, 235–240; facsimile reprint in Michael Redclift and Graham Woodgate, eds., The Sociology of the Environment, vol. 2 (Aldershot: Edward Elgar, 1995), item 33.

verification.note: Author-hosted scan of the Redclift and Woodgate 1995 facsimile read (contents list gives the item as Radical Ecology, 235–40). Original page heads visible; pages assigned from running heads: contributions of radical theorists, including 'Science is not a process of discovering ultimate truths of nature, but a social construction' (p. 236); 'Radical ecology lacks coherence as a theory and as a movement' (p. 237); the book's chapters organised around 'a framework that uses the concepts of ecology, production, reproduction, and consciousness in understanding both the ecological crisis and ways of overcoming it' and two contradictions, production–ecology and production–reproduction (p. 239); ecofeminists 'press for gender equality and the subordination of production to the reproduction of life' (p. 240). Rest of the book unread. Open Library work OL2911260W (Routledge).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period: the framework carried into an analysis of environmental movements.

new_sources.title: Carolyn Merchant, “The Death of Nature: A Retrospective,” Organization & Environment 11, no. 2 (June 1998): 198–206.
new_sources.citation: Carolyn Merchant, “The Death of Nature: A Retrospective,” Organization & Environment 11:2 (1998): 198–206. doi:10.1177/0921810698112008.

verification.note: Author-hosted scan OCR'd and read pp. 198–202 in full and the start of the review appendix (pp. 202–204); Crossref 10.1177/0921810698112008 confirms volume, issue and pages. Influences: Hessen and Zilsel, Leiss's Domination of Nature (p. 199); Roszak, and 'It was Kubrin’s idea that the key concept of early modern science was that matter was dead' (p. 200). Her summary of the early reviews, including objections over 'how historical events were related to each other and especially to ideas' and 'the precise relationship between female metaphors that described nature and the social subjection of women' (p. 201). Ecological Revolutions as 'a model of revolutionary transformations based on ecology, production, reproduction, and consciousness'; Radical Ecology and Earthcare (p. 202). Her own account of her reception, written inside the period; not independent evidence of it.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period self-account: sources of the 1980 argument and early objections, as she reports them.

new_sources.title: Theodore Steinberg, review of Carolyn Merchant, Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (1989), Technology and Culture 32, no. 2 (April 1991): 398–399.
new_sources.citation: Theodore Steinberg, review of Merchant, Ecological Revolutions, Technology and Culture 32:2, part 1 (1991): 398–399. doi:10.1353/tech.1991.0103.

verification.note: Read in full in the Project MUSE PDF (article 888747), OCR'd because the text layer is unreadable. Merchant's 'work has played an important role in forging the field'; the book's definition of ecological revolutions (book pp. 2–3); 'An imbalance between the forces of production and reproduction spurred the shift to the capitalist mode of production'; 'Patriarchy ... had come into conflict with ecology' (book p. 187); 18th-century cosmos with 'rocks and minerals as living, growing things' (book p. 143) (p. 398). 'the book’s theorizing about ecological and social change—especially its integration of gender into the analysis—is a signal contribution. But Merchant’s quest for theoretical rigor may have come at the expense of a more nuanced, richly textured narrative. There are painfully few people making history in this book' (p. 399).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period review: praise for the gender analysis and criticism of the narrative.

new_sources.title: William Cronon, “The Uses of Environmental History,” Environmental History Review 17, no. 3 (Fall 1993): 1–22.
new_sources.citation: William Cronon, “The Uses of Environmental History,” Environmental History Review 17:3 (1993): 1–22 (ASEH presidential address).

verification.note: Author-hosted scan OCR'd; pp. 2–3, 8–9 and notes 5, 13 and 18 read for Merchant. 'Carolyn Merchant joined Worster in bringing an environmentalist perspective to the history of science, but combined it with a more feminist approach to argue in The Death of Nature that western science has harmed nature and women in parallel ways; her Radical Ecology, though less historical, is still more activist in its efforts to intervene in contemporary political struggles' (p. 3; n. 5). Lesson footnoted to Death of Nature and Ecological Revolutions (n. 18): 'Men and women often experience the world in very different ways, so that one cannot hope to understand the way a culture relates to an environment without examining the ways it engenders the natural world' (p. 9). Other agents drafting 1.131 entries may cite the same essay under another id; merge at release.

new_sources.title: Melissa Leach and Cathy Green, “Gender and Environmental History: From Representation of Women and Nature to Gender Analysis of Ecology and Politics,” Environment and History 3, no. 3 (1997): 343–370.
new_sources.citation: Melissa Leach and Cathy Green, “Gender and Environmental History,” Environment and History 3:3 (1997): 343–370. doi:10.3197/096734097779555818.

verification.note: Open-access PDF (Environment & Society Portal) read pp. 343–349 and references. They criticise ecofeminist and 'women, environment and development' histories. The Scientific Revolution 'is taken by many ecofeminists as the time in western history when both women and nature were conceptually devalued (Merchant 1982; Plumwood 1986; Warren 1987)', quoting the 'death of nature' sentence (p. 346); they also quote Merchant's Radical Ecology (1992: 192) describing cultural ecofeminism (p. 346); 'The key feature of the ecofeminist “histories” ... is the way that femininity is linked a priori both “with nature” and “with the past”' (p. 348), said chiefly of Shiva. They do not discuss Merchant's reproduction framework. The remaining case-study sections (Africa, India) were not read.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period criticism of ecofeminist history, including The Death of Nature as an example.

later_readings_not_added.mcneill_2003: J. R. McNeill, 'Observations on the Nature and Culture of Environmental History,' History and Theory 42 (2003): 5–43, read pp. 38–39 (williamcronon.net H701_McNeill.pdf): 'Carolyn Merchant has offered a more formal theory that tries to take gender into account, and which avoids the notion that women are inherently closer to nature. It adds another variable to that of the Worster-McEvoy trio, inserting reproduction (meaning both human biological and social reproduction and non-human biological reproduction) into the mix. Whatever the merits of this scheme, it has not attracted wide imitation within environmental history. The signal contribution, I think, of Merchant (and others) is to insist that historians consider the variable experiences of males and females' (pp. 38–39); n. 135 locates the construct in chapter 1 of Ecological Revolutions. Quoted in edge 1 as a labelled later reading; not added as a source here because other 1.131 drafts are likely to add McNeill 2003. If none does, add it at release and cite it on edge 1. Fix pass 2026-10-13 (sol-review-1.131): McNeill 2003 is a new source in the extras packet (pe131_extras_mcneill_2003, canonical after the batch merges); it is now in edge 1's source_ids, and its pp. 38–39 wording was re-checked in the text-layer PDF.
